questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Due to covid it wasn't possible for me to go to either Canada or Australia, to do what I love most: skiing and surfing. Therefore I chose the next best thing, which was to get as close as possible to the mountains within the borders of Europe, and hopefully get to ski a bit during my excahnge. 
At the same time I wanted to do my exchange in a country with a culture and climate very different from Denmark to expand my horizon and actually feel like being away from home. Therefore Milan in northern Italy seemed like the best choice for me. And it certainly was.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It wasn't the easiest thing in the world to find my schedule, so I missed my first lecture, but it wasn't the end of the world. You just have to be patient and read the emails you receive, and there is most likely someone to write if you are missing some information, but everything is a bit slower in Italy - they rarely stress, so you shouldn't either.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
All the assistance regarding the academics was via email, which worked fine, but you have to be patient. Might have been due to Covid, but I'm not sure. 
But there is a great student organisation called Erasmus students network (ESN), who plans an intro week with a lot of activities and you can always reach out to them as well for help, but mostly regarding non-academic stuff. There weren't any tour of the university or so, as it has many different campus in the city.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I chose to book an airbnb with a friend from home a couple of months before arrival. This worked very well, so I can definitely recommend it. We chose to do it this way, to avoid the stress about finding a place to live after arrival, and because we were two persons who knew each other from home, so it was easy to find an airbnb in the right size and to a fair price. Also by using airbnb we avoided signing any contracts. 
With that said, a lot of people chose to find housing after arrival, and start out at a hostel or something like that, which seemed to work fine for them.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
It isn't cheap to live in Milan, but I would say the prices are quite similar to Copenhagen. The metro works very well in Milan and covers most of the city, so it is definitely nice to live close to a metro station instead of tram or buses, which is a bit more unreliable timewise. I lived a bit outside the center, but right next to a metro station (Cimiano), so it was still easy to get in to the center in a reasonable time. 

Most people I knew lived in the eastern or southern part of the city, which is some nice areas. Citta studi is in the east, and a lot of the students live here. It is next to the area called Porta Venezia, which I really liked - a lot of nice cafes, restaurants and bars.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Be aware of the rules when living in a student accommodation. In most dorms you are only allowed to have one friend visiting at a time, and they have to leave before 00.00 in the evening, because they are not allowed to sleep there. You often share a room with a roomate, and there is a receptionist/security at the entrance at all hours controlling, who you bring in.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was difficult to find out which courses were in english and italian, and to plan your schedule with as little overlap in classes as possible.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I was strongly recommended to follow a master programme, in order to avoid the overlap of classes. This I did but I chose to only take two out of three of the courses from this program, as the last one didn't fit my education. Therefore I had to find one more course which didn't overlap too much with the other program, and one that was taught in english and with the correct amount of credits.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not much help, other than the recommendation to follow the master program, but it is possible to email the professors and ask them questions about their course.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got what I wanted, but had to change my original choice of the third course, as it overlapped too much and all of sudden was taught in italian instead of english as the website said.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Take it easy and don't stress too much about it. You have plenty of time to change your courses if you aren't satisfied or run in to other complications.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I wasn't prepared for the heavy italian accent, that all professors have. Sometimes it made it difficult to follow the lectures, but with help from some hopefully good slides, I managed to understand most parts. It takes some time to get used to, and all professors have their own pronunciation of certain words, which you learn to tune in to.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took master courses in order to have english lectures. The syllabus was big, but the level was fair even though I wasn't a master student yet.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: We only had lectures, so I really missed some classes with task solving or journal club, because I don't learn very well from just listening. Therefore the exam preparation was heavier than expected, as it felt like I had to learn everything from scratch, but I guess it's different from person to person, how they learn best. Also, we didn't have any text books, so we didn't have to prepare anything for the lectures, so I didn't do any self studying before the exam preparations.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Pathogenetic basis of disease
Applied pharmacology to biotechnology 
Communicable and non-communicable diseases

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Pathogenetic basis of disease is a very big course for 12 credits about a lot of different diseases from cancer to cardiovascular diseases, which was quite interesting. Our exam was multiple choice, but in Italy there is no guarantee that the exam form is the same from year to year. 

Applied pharmacology to biotechnology was more focused on methods of diagnosing and drug-treatment. Both traditional drug treatment like iboprofen and the problems regarding this, but also new methods like RNA interference and monoclonal antibodies. A big part concerned use of fluorescent tools as biosensors. The exam was oral. 

Communicable and non-communicable diseases was the third course outside the master program. Again concerning many different diseases, like diabetes and cardiovascular diseases, but also infectious diseases. Some of the syllabus overlapped with pathogenetic basis of disease, but that wasn't a problem - only nice with some repetition. The exam was an oral one with one professor, and a written multiple choice with the two other professors.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
My wallet got stolen in the metro, with some cash. Later my phone got stolen as well but on the street, but my insurance covered it. Be aware of your bag always, and don't put anything in your pockets. 

Personal spending includes about six trips to other parts of Italy, like Sicily, the Dolomites, Cinque Terre and Venice.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Going out to restaurants and bars is less expensive than Denmark. The same for alcohol in general. Supermarket prices are fairly the same. Taxis and public transportation is cheaper as well.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The organisation that I mentioned earlier, ESN, is really big and active for my university (La Statale) in Milan. It is run by other students who volunteer to make the Erasmus students stay in Milan as good as possible. They planned all kinds of activities during the entire stay; beach volley, wine dinners, aperitivos, day trips to nearby cities, museum trips, city tours and many other things. If you buy the ESN card for 10 euros, you are allowed to participate in all of it.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: All of them, especially in the beginning. It is a great way to meet other people fast and make friends, who you can plan your own trips and activities with. And you can really feel how engaged the volunteers of ESN are in making this the best time of our lives.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Visit nearby cities! It is easy to get around with train. 

I really liked Cinque Terre, which was extremely beautiful. ESN has a trip to Rome for alle Erasmus students in Italy, which was a lot of fun as well. If you don't get a spot you can also go there by train yourself. Venice was amazing as well, but we waited until January to visit this city to avoid the big crowds of tourists, which was definitely the right choice. And go on the Snow Week Erasmus skiing trip as well! It was amazing.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was a bit difficult to adjust in the beginning, but Italians are very nice people. Some doesn't speak english, but it wasn't a big problem.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Be prepared for the Italian lifestyle! Organizing, planning and deadline are not their best skills, to put it nicely. You have to be patient, and don't stress too much about deadlines, because they don't.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Their laid back life style which also includes authorities including the university and the police - I spent 4 hours at the police station in the waiting room only to fill out a paper and hand it in, which took less than 10 min. Also most police don't speak english. 
We also had to be very patient regarding our exam dates. In Italy the students communicate with the professors trying to find a suitable date for the exam. And then the professors talk about it and then get back to the students. So it is a long process, but the bright side is, that you can choose between a couple of dates and not just one. 
You get used to the laid backness eventually.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The eating and winery. I loved all the italian food and wine. It's a big part of being italian.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Be patient always. Don't stress too much, cause italians never do, and enjoy the country, explore as much as you can.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No, everything has been said.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Experiencing Italy, but not just from a vacation point of view but as a citizen. Also made me appreciate the danish culture a bit more and really expanded my horizon.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I found it difficult sometimes to be away from my family and home, and always feeling a bit like a stranger, because I didn't speak italian and doesn't look italian at all. But you get used to it as well, and eventually feel more familiar with the city and also the language if you take the language course. At the end an italian even asked me for directions, which felt like a little win :))

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Bring clothes for summer and winter and explore the city and country as much as possible. Don't stress about uni too much - the professors are quite flexible with Erasmus students, so take advantage of that.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
